# Efficient logical operations in quantum LDPC codes using simple resource states

Quantum LDPC codes provide a substantial reduction in qubit overhead required for fault-tolerant quantum computation compared to surface code, thanks to their high encoding rate. However, operating simultaneously on multiple logical qubits encoded in the same block is more challenging and may slow down logical operations. Prior work addresses this problem by designing complex resource states to perform logical measurements in LDPC codes. Here, we propose an approach that only consumes cat states. Whereas previous work on cat-based measurements focuses on a single logical measurement, we design a protocol for the joint measurement of l commuting logical operators. The key ingredient is the design of a scheduler code determining the measurement sequence and allowing for the decoding of all logical measurement outcomes. Numerical simulations with the LDPC codes Q70 and Q102 of the walking cat architecture show a reduction of nearly 3× in the number of cat-based measurements required versus the Viterbi method for measuring l = 20 commuting logical operators. Combining our logical measurement protocols with a new variant of the CliNR partial error correction scheme, we achieve a reduction of up to 73× versus the Viterbi method for random Clifford circuits. Our approach also applies to non-Clifford gates, producing a reduction of up to 5× versus the Viterbi method for Toffoli gates.

A quantum error correction code lies at the core of any fault-tolerant quantum computer (FTQC) architecture. Motivated by theoretical breakthroughs [1–4], promising numerical results [5–10], architecture studies [11–17], and experimental realizations [18, 19], quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes are gaining traction. In contrast to surface codes, they encode many logical qubits in the same block, reducing the qubit-overhead. However, this encoding makes logical qubits harder to access because operating simultaneously on logical qubits supported on the same block is challenging, resulting in a potential slowdown of logical operations. Substantial effort has been invested in the design of fault-tolerant logical measurements for quantum LDPC codes based on graph-based resource states [20–29]. This approach has three main limitations (a) It relies on complex resource states and for each logical measurement, a new code is formed, merging the memory with the resource state, imposing stringent hardware requirements to accommodate all these merged codes. (b) These protocols are typically described in terms of homological algebra which is a beautiful formalism but may be less accessible for part of the community unfamiliar with this framework. (c) Finally, these protocols are mostly studied through asymptotic proofs of fault-tolerance and their practical performance needs further investigation. To remove the need for complex resource states, we leverage Shor’s measurement scheme which only consumes cat states |0 . . . 0⟩ + |1 . . . 1⟩ [30]. Each cat state interacts with the memory only for a single time step, before it is measured, removing the need to form a merge code. The exact protocol is easy to understand ∗ Corresponding author: mark.webster@ionq.co by inspecting the circuit without additional formalism. Furthermore, we focus on the practical regime and we leverage the fact that fault-tolerance is not required to achieve the target logical error rate required for a specific quantum algorithm. Our approach requires bringing cat states next to the qubits to measure, making this protocol well-suited for moving qubits such as trapped ions [31], neutral atoms [32], spin qubits [33] or electrons floating

Shor’s method was originally proposed for the measurement of syndrome bits and improved in [35–37]. The walking cat architecture demonstrates the practicality of cat-based measurements for logical measurements in quantum LDPC codes [17]. Therein, the measurement of a logical operator is performed through a Viterbi measurement which reaches a target accuracy. In this work, we design substantially more efficient cat-based logical measurement protocols by combining the measurement of l commuting logical operators. Our main innovation is the introduction of a scheduler code that determines the sequence of cat-based measurements and enables the joint decoding of all the measurement outcomes. To illustrate our results, we consider the quantum LDPC codes Q70 and Q102 from the walking cat architecture. The measurement of l = 10 and 20 commuting logical operators consumes respectively an average of only 2.1 and 1.7 cat states per logical measurement. Our results also apply to trivial logical measurement, that is stabilizers, which leads to a protocol for preparation of a stabilizer state through the measurement of its stabilizer

We introduce a new variant of the CliNR partial error correction scheme [38, 39] which leverages our logical measurement protocols to improve the efficiency of logical Toffoli gates and logical Clifford gates. For Q70 and Q102, we obtain a 4.2× and 5.1× reduction respectively in the number of cat-based measurements required verarXiv:2607.16166v3 [quant-ph] 18 Nov 2026

sus the Viterbi method for Toffoli gates and a 18.6× and 73.1× reduction for random Clifford operations. This application of CliNR is unexpected because CliNR was originally designed for partial error correction but the original scheme leads to an increase in execution time. To achieve these results, we execute part of the scheme at the logical level and other parts at the physical level. Moreover, we leverage our logical measurement protocols to improve the efficiency of resource state preparation and verification for the CliNR scheme. II. PREVIOUS WORK ON MEASUREMENT OUTCOMES AND CLASSICAL CODES The idea of protecting measurement outcomes with a classical code has a long history. Fujiwara first observed that redundant stabilizer measurements can be used to protect syndrome data against measurement errors [40]. This led to the framework of data-syndrome codes, where data and syndrome errors are corrected jointly [41, 42]. It was later connected to the single-shot properties of

The same principle has been applied to logical measurements. Sequences of logical measurements encoded with a classical code were discussed in [35] for small block codes. In [45] temporally encoded lattice surgery (TELS) measures a set of commuting logical Pauli operators, together with redundant products of them chosen from a classical code. This allows timelike failures in surface-code lattice surgery to be detected, so fewer syndrome rounds are needed per lattice-surgery operation. More recently, [46] used timelike Reed–Solomon protection against measurement errors in a Shor-style syndrome extraction scheme for Galois qudits concatenated over high-rate LDPC codes. Our protocol differs from these works in three ways. First, the scheduler code can be used for error correction as well as detection: the decoder recovers all l logical measurement outcomes, rather than flagging a failure and repeating the measurement. Secondly, we target quantum LDPC codes with many logical qubits per block using cat states for logical measurements and use simulation results for these codes indicating that measurement outcomes suffer from independent bit flip errors [17]. Thirdly, we give an algorithm for choosing the scheduler code to minimize the number of cat-based measurements required to meet a desired logical error rate. III. BACKGROUND: MEASUREMENT OF A

Our primitive operation is a cat-based measurement which performs the measurement of a w-qubit Pauli operator using a w-qubit cat state. Following [17], we assume that a cat-based measurement can be executed at each syndrome extraction cycle (SEC) and that measurement outcomes suffer from independent bit-flips with flip rate pF . An optimized cat state preparation scheme is described in [17], which also verifies numerically the independence of cat-based measurement flips. We expect this assumption to hold for quantum LDPC codes with

A measurement protocol takes as input a set of l target Pauli operators to measure. It specifies a schedule of m measurements which may be a product of the target Paulis and which have sufficient redundancy to cater for measurement flip errors. Measurement flip errors are represented by a vector e ∈ {0, 1}m with distribution P (e) = pwt(e) F (1 − pF )m−wt(e). The physical measurement outcomes resulting from the schedule produce a binary outcome vector v of length m. The outcome vector is used to calculate the most likely logical outcome vector ˆu of length l. The protocol must include enough measurements to ensure that the probability of any logical measurement being incorrect is less than the target

In [17] three protocols for measurement of a single logical Pauli are introduced which we extend to sets of multiple commuting Paulis in this work. The first is the error detected measurement protocol (EDM) where the target Pauli is measured m times in each attempt. If all measurement outcomes are the same, the protocol succeeds. Otherwise, the protocol is restarted. Providing m > log ε/ log pF , the target logical error rate is achieved. In the error corrected measurement protocol (ECM), a single attempt of m measurements is conducted and the most likely outcome is selected by majority vote. For this protocol to meet the target logical error rate, m must satisfy P wt(e)≤(m−1)/2 P (e) > 1 − ε. The Viterbi measurement protocol is similar to the ECM protocol but terminates as soon as |m − 2m1| > log(ε−1 − 1)/ log(p−1 F − 1) where m1 is the weight of the outcome vector v. We use the Viterbi measurement protocol as the base case for comparison with our new multi-Pauli measurement protocols as it requires the lowest number of cat-based measurements on average of these methods. A. Scheduler Matrices and Codes In the MEDM and MECM protocols we measure l independent commuting Pauli operators P0, . . . , Pl−1 using a measurement schedule specified by an l × m generator matrix G. We refer to G as the scheduler matrix, and

to the binary linear code generated by G as the scheduler code, denoted ⟨G⟩. The number of columns in G, |G| = m, is the number of measurements in the schedule. Each row of G corresponds to one of the target Paulis to be measured. Each column of G corresponds to a product of the target Pauli operators so that the jth measurement is Qj := Q 0≤i<l P Gij i . The measurement outcome vector v is of length m and the jth entry corresponds to the measurement outcome of Qj . We require that the first l columns of G form an information set (i.e., a maximum set of independent columns of G) which allows us to infer the logical measurement outcome u in the absence of error such that v = uG. If G is in systematic form G = [I|A], u is determined by taking the first l bits of v.

We generalize the EDM protocol to a set of l commuting Paulis by using an l × m scheduler matrix G. After m measurements, we use the rank m − l check matrix H satisfying GH T = 0 to detect errors. In this section we show how to choose a scheduler code which minimizes the average number of cat-based measurements required by the truncated MECM protocol. Let the number of cat-based measurements required for the error e in the truncated MECM protocol be me. The average number of cat-based measurements for the truncated MECM protocol is mAvg = P e meP (e). Where mpF ≪ 1, the highest contributor to mAvg is the number of cat-based measurements m0 required for the allzero error string. For the all-zero error, the measurement outcome vector is a codeword of form v = uG. In this case, the protocol terminates once the posterior probability 1 − P (u|v) = UER⟨G⟩/(P (0) + UER⟨G⟩) < ε which is the same condition as in Equation (2). To minimize the average number of cat-based measurements for the truncated MECM protocol, we use a scheduler matrix of form G = [G0|G1]. For G0 we choose the code with the smallest block size meeting the UER condition in Equation (2). This guarantees that the truncated MECM protocol terminates at the last column of

G0 for e = 0 and so m0 = |G0| and is minimal. We then choose the smallest G1 that has distance sufficiently large to guarantee that G := [G0|G1] satisfies LER⟨G⟩ < ε. LOGICAL CLIFFORD AND TOFFOLI GATES Here, we propose a new protocol for logical Clifford gates, and we apply it to build more efficent logical Toffoli gates through their Clifford + T decomposition. Logical Clifford gates are implemented through the CliNR scheme [38] executed at the logical level. Recall that CliNR works in three steps: resource state preparation (RSP), resource state verification (RSV) and resource state injection (RSI) represented in Fig. 1(a). The efficiency of the protocol originates from (i) replacing a Clifford circuit by the offline preparation of a resource state (RSP), which can be prepared using error detection instead of error correction, (ii) preparing and verifying the CliNR resource state using an MEDM, merging RSP and RSV, (iii) implementing RSI through physical operations (transversal CNOT gates and destructive measurements) to avoid the time penalty of RSI in the original CliNR

CliNR Protocol for Physical Clifford Circuits The CliNR protocol applies a physical Clifford operation C by preparing a resource stabilizer state offline on auxiliary blocks A and B. The auxiliary blocks are initialized in Bell states and C is applied to auxiliary block B using noisy gate-based operations. To validate preparation of the resource state, a selection of stabilizers is measured using an auxiliary qubit (MC in Figure 1a). If any of the stabilizer measurements are non-zero, the protocol restarts. Otherwise, the Clifford gate is applied via state injection using a transversal CNOT between the data block and auxiliary block A and measurements in the X and Z basis on the data block and auxiliary block A respectively. The output |Cψ⟩ is teleported to auxiliary

In this section, we present simulation results for the MEDM and MECM protocols of Sections IV B and IV C, as well as the logical CliNR protocol of Section V B. In [17] the authors demonstrate numerically that measurement flip errors for the Q70 and Q102 codes can be modeled as an independent bit flip channel with rate pF = C1wp where C1 = 2.1 is a constant, w is the cat state size and p is the error rate of 2-qubit gates for the device. For our results, we use a flip rate of pF = 6.3 × 10−3 corresponding to a physical error rate of p = 10−4 and cat state size w = 30. We use the target logical error rate of ε = 10−10. The metric we use for comparison is the number of cat-based measurements required by the protocol. In Table I we give a high-level summary for the MEDM, MECM, and logical CliNR protocols. To achieve a logical error rate of ε = 10−10, the Viterbi protocol of Section III requires almost 2.4 times as many catbased measurements as the MECM protocol for measuring l = 10 commuting Paulis and almost 3 times as many for l = 20 commuting Paulis. The MEDM protocol requires only 1.81 cat-based measurements per target Pauli and the MECM only 1.71 cat-based measurements (see Tables II and III). For full details of simulation methodology, see Section C 1. We then simulated logical CliNR using truncated MEDM for stabilizer state preparation. We compared the number of cat-based measurements required for logical CliNR to the number required by the Viterbi gatebased protocol. The Viterbi gate-based protocol involves synthesizing a logical Clifford into logical single and twoqubit gates, which are then implemented via logical measurements. Each logical measurement is performed using the Viterbi measurement protocol (see Section A). We considered two scenarios - the Toffoli circuit requiring four logical qubits as set out in Figure 4 and a set of 100 randomly generated Clifford operators. For each scenario, we simulated using the Q70 code with 6 logical qubits and the Q102 code with 22 logical qubits from [17]. We found that the Viterbi gate-based protocol requires up to 5.1x more cat-based measurements than MEDM CliNR for Toffoli circuits. For random Clifford circuits the advantage is even larger, and this scenario illustrates the scope of potential gains from the MEDM CliNR protocol. For full details of simulation methodology and

In this analysis we focused on establishing the reliability of the classical logical-measurement decoding problem rather than including all possible sources of faults, for instance in the transversal CNOT, destructive measurements, data-block creation, and qubit transport. The reason for this is that analysis of these effects is very device-dependent and the CliNR protocol is applicable to any device with access to transversal CNOT and catbased measurements. We also note the flexibility of the protocol and that accuracy can be tuned by modifying the target logical error rate if necessary.

We have presented methods to improve the efficiency of logical measurements, Clifford gates, and non-Clifford Toffoli gates in quantum LDPC codes. In future work, it would be interesting to investigate which features of quantum LDPC codes are sufficient to ensure independence of cat-based measurement outcomes. Another open question is the design of explicit families of scheduler codes instead of selecting codes with the best-knowndistance. Finally, the minimal space and time footprint of our logical operations makes them an ideal target for near-term experimental demonstration.

1. Clifford Operations via Frame Tracking In the walking cat architecture [17], logical Clifford operators are implemented where possible via frame tracking. This method does not require any physical operations but instead involves maintaining a Pauli frame. For a code block with k logical qubits, the Pauli frame is a tableau comprising a binary 2k × 2k symplectic matrix and a length 2k vector which represents a logical Pauli basis with signs (see [55]). When a logical Clifford operator C is applied, the tableau is updated by conjugating the logical Pauli basis by C. Not all logical Clifford operations can be implemented via frame tracking and this means that they need to be implemented physically. For instance, frame tracking can only be applied efficiently for operations within the same code block. Frame tracking also requires that each element of the logical Pauli basis is accessible in the sense that cat-based measurements are possible within architecture constraints. 2. Accessibility of Logical Pauli Measurements Here we describe the accessibility of logical Pauli measurements in more detail. A key parameter of the walking cat architecture is the maximum cat state size w which can be produced by the cat factory. Within a code block, only Pauli operators of weight w or less can be measured using cat states. The minimum weight representative of a logical Pauli with binary symplectic representation v for a quantum stabilizer code with check matrix H is the element of the coset v + ⟨H⟩ with minimum symplectic weight. A logical Pauli measurement is accessible if the Pauli has a minimum weight representative with weight w or less. Accessibility depends on the QECC used - for Q70 all logical Paulis have representatives with weight ≤ 18 but for Q102 some logical Paulis have minimum

Where all logical Cliffords are not guaranteed to be accessible, only single qubit logical Cliffords (generated by ⟨H, S⟩) and logical qubit permutations can be implemented via frame tracking. Enumerating these and checking for minimum weight representatives is far less challenging than for general logical Paulis because there are 2k+1 CSS logical operators versus 22k logical Paulis in total. Where a Clifford operation cannot be implemented via frame tracking, the Viterbi gate-based protocol is used (see Figure 2). The input to this protocol is a logical Clifford operator, which we decompose into a circuit of one and two-qubit logical Clifford gates (see [55, 57–59]). Single-qubit logical Clifford gates can be implemented using two logical Pauli measurements, and two-qubit gates using three logical Pauli measurements as set out in Figure 2. Each logical Pauli measurement is implemented using cat-based measurements interleaved with SEC rounds using the Viterbi measurement protocol of Section III. 2. Lookup Decoder and LER of Classical Codes In this section, we show how to construct a lookup decoder for a binary linear code with l×m generator matrix G. This produces an ideal maximum likelihood decoder which is used for simulations of the MECM protocol and to calculate the logical error rate of binary linear codes exactly. The decoder works by specifying a minimal coset leader ˆe for each coset v + ⟨G⟩. The lookup decoder applies the correction ˆe for any element of the coset. The coset leader is the element of the coset which is of minimum weight (and so highest probability) and minimum lexicographical order (so that we have a total order for each coset). There are 2m−l coset leaders and these can be calculated in O(2m) binary vector operations as follows. Assuming the first l columns of G form an information set, we put G into systematic form using Gaussian elimination so that GS = [I|A] and ⟨GS ⟩ = ⟨G⟩. The complementary space is generated by C = [0|Im−l].

The lookup decoder takes as input a binary vector v of length m. We identify the error coset by adding rows of GS to eliminate the first l entries of v and this allows us to identify the coset by the last m − l entries of the resulting vector. The correction is the coset leader of the

This process allows us to identify the correctable errors for the code ⟨G⟩ using an ideal decoder. The decoder successfully corrects any error which corresponds to a coset leader, but any other error gives a logical error. The exact methods for calculating coset probabilities of Section B 1 have exponential complexity in l, m. For large codes, we instead use heuristic methods. The random information set algorithm for distance-finding [61– 63] can be modified to sample from low-weight elements of the coset v + ⟨G⟩. As low-weight elements have the highest contribution to the coset probability, this gives an estimate of the coset probability. By returning the lowest weight element with least lexicographic order, this method can also be used as a heuristic decoder. The method is set out in Algorithm 1. The function RREF(Gv , ix) performs reduced row echelon using the column order specified by the vector ix and on average returns low weight vectors (see [64]). The wLexMin function returns the minimal vector by weight then lexicographic order.

In the walking cat architecture, we would interleave each measurement with an SEC round and may require a final SEC at the end of the protocol, but we do not explicitly consider these here. Measurements may also be subject to a cat missing error but for simplicity we omit this effect in this work. This has only a small effect on the number of cat-based measurements required because cat state preparation rarely fails [17]. Both protocols have relative advantages and are likely to be useful in different contexts. The MECM protocol can be used directly on logical blocks without restarting and has a slightly lower average number of cat-based measurements. On the other hand, the MEDM protocol does not require a decoder so it is less complex to model and run. Selecting an optimal generator matrix for the MEDM protocol depends on the undetectable error rate which is less complex to calculate exactly and we have closed form expressions for the key NAvg, mN and mAvg

Accessibility in MEDM/MECM We now show how to adapt the MEDM and MECM protocols of Sections IV B and IV C to take into account accessibility constraints set out in Section A for logical Pauli measurements. We assume that a logical Pauli basis B has been selected and that any product of w basis elements is accessible. Let Pi, 0 ≤ i < l be a set of independent commuting Paulis we wish to measure. Any product of the Pi can be expressed uniquely as a product of elements of B and stabilizer generators of the code. The logical weight is the number of elements of B in the

To ensure accessibility, we choose an l × m scheduler matrix G whose columns represent accessible Paulis. To maximize the efficiency of the MEDM and MECM schemes, the code generated by G should have a low undetectable error rate. We first enumerate all elements of the group generated by the target Paulis and calculate their logical weight. Products of the Pi are represented as length l binary vectors in the same way as set out in Section IV A. Let Cw be the set of binary vectors representing products of the Pi which have logical weight at most w. By choosing the columns of G from the vectors in Cw, we ensure that all measurements in the schedule

The next step is to choose l vectors from Cw which form an information set. This is done using matroid partitioning techniques [65],[66] and if no such information set exists, the algorithm fails. Otherwise, let u be the integer vector indexing the vectors in Cw which form the

The remaining m − l columns of G can now be chosen to give a low undetectable error rate. We use an evolutionary algorithm based on the method in [67]. The individuals in the algorithm are represented as integer vectors of length m − l which index the rows of Cw. The initial population is a set of randomly generated vectors vi. The fitness function for vi is 1 − UER⟨Gi ⟩ where the columns of Gi are the columns of Cw indexed by u|vi. In each round, we select the vi with highest fitness. Mutation is done by choosing a entry in vi at random and replacing it with an integer in [0, .., |Cw| − 1]. We also considered greedy and A* algorithms for optimization but found these challenging to apply due to the large number of columns typically required for the scheduler

We then verify the logical action by tracking how logical Xi and logical Zi in the data block D is mapped to block B. Firstly, we note that both auxiliary blocks A and B are prepared in a logical |0⟩ states so they are stabilized by each element of S acting on their respective blocks. The measurements in MC are logical measurements and SEC rounds are done in between these which ensure that block B remains in the codespace. The corrections R and Q are both products of logical Pauli operators and so do not take block B out of the codespace. Hence, block B is stabilized by elements of S throughout the protocol. We now consider the situation where logical CliNR is applied in the middle of an operation where logical Cliffords have been applied via frame tracking (see Section A). In this case, let F be the accumulated Clifford operations applied via frame tracking. Via frame tracking, the logical Pauli X operators have been mapped to F XiF −1 and F ZiF −1. These are not guaranteed to be CSS logical Paulis so the measurement of physical X and Z operators may not suffice to infer the logical X and Z measurement values required by the protocol. The solution is to absorb frame tracking into the Clifford C to be applied via logical CliNR so that we implement CF . This ensures that we are working in the original CSS Pauli basis and means that logical X and Z measurement values can be inferred from physical X and Z measurements. After applying logical CliNR in this way, the Pauli frame has been ‘cleared’ and we are again working in the original CSS Pauli basis.

Accessibility in Logical CliNR We now show how to adapt the logical CliNR protocol of Section V B to take into account accessibility constraints set out in Section A for logical Pauli measurements. We assume logical width w so that any product of w elements of the logical Pauli basis is accessible and that any CSS logical operator is accessible (see Section A). The first step is to use Aaronson and Gottesman Clifford circuit synthesis [55] to break the desired logical Clifford into three types of layers - those including only S, only Hadamard and only CNOT operators. The maximum number of layers in such a decomposition is 11, but many Clifford circuits of interest can be implemented in far fewer layers. We now show how to implement each type of layer in a way which guarantees that each stabilizer measurement in the CliNR protocol is accessible. To implement a circuit involving only S operators, we use the CZNR protocol of Section D 2. To prepare the stabilizer state on the auxiliary block, we must measure logical Paulis of form SiXiS−1 i = Yi. Measurements can be done one at a time using the Viterbi protocol or jointly using MEDM/MECM using a scheduler matrix with maximum column weight w. To implement a circuit involving only H operators, we use the CliNR protocol of Section V B. The stabilizers to be measured in step MC are of form MX,i = XA,iZB,i and MZ,i = ZA,iXB,i. Any product of the MX,i is a CSS logical when restricted to auxiliary block A or block B. CSS Paulis are accessible by assumption so these can be measured jointly using MEDM/MECM. The same applies to the MZ,i so we apply the MEDM/MECM protocol separately to products of the MZ,i. For the CliNR protocol, we also calculated a low-weight representative for each stabilizer acting on auxiliary block B and verified that it was at most weight 18 for Q70 and 30 for Q102. Full results of the simulations are set out in Table VIII. We see that implementing logical CliNR using Viterbi measurements of each of the stabilizers of the resource state requires between 2.2 and 2.6 times more cat-based measurements than implementing these using the MEDM protocol - this is consistent with the results of Table II. We see a further gain when comparing the CliNR MEDM protocol with the Viterbi gate-based protocol. This is because CliNR involves offline preparation of a resource stabilizer state which requires only 2l logical measurements where l is the number of qubits in the support of the logical Clifford. Note that this is the same as the bound in [56]. The asymptotic bound on the number of 2-qubit gates required is O(l2/ log l), each of which requires 3 logical measurements (see [55]).
